messages.author: 17f8070912132195
messages.subject: Smooth functions like GAMs
parts:
Dear all, 

I am wondering if R-INLA provides any methods to fit a smooth effect as GAMs do. I found that Cosandey-Godin, Krainski, Worm, and Mills Flemming (2014) used a 'rw1' to get the smooth effect of bathymetry. They stated that "This is equivalent to a smooth function used in GAMs." 

I am confused if  'ar1', 'rw2' etc. can achieve the same goal.

Thanks,
Ruby

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Smooth functions like GAMs
parts:
The INLA models _are_ GAMs, so I think their wording is a bit unfortunate. I think what you’re really asking is whether the smoothing models in specific frequentist GAM software have correspondences in the R-INLA software, and the answer is yes.
 rw1,ar1, correspond to 1st order spline penalty models, and rw2 corresponds to 2nd order splines.  The main difference is that in frequentist methods it’s mostly the penalized likelihood mode that’s considered, and in Bayesian methods there is a greater emphasis on the Gaussian process aspect of the models.

Finn

messages.author: ee8358804ba614e0
messages.subject: Re: Smooth functions like GAMs
parts:
In the mgcv package is a function smoothCon, which allows you to extract the basis functions of any smoother. You can then use these as covariates in INLA.

Alternatively, you can write the smoother as X * b + Z * u, where the u's are random effects. Its variance determines the smoothness of the smoother (at the price of a hyperparameter). Works quite well.

Alain Zuur

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Smooth functions like GAMs
parts:
Independent weights for the basis functions only gives the right model if the basis functions were constructed to allow that. It’s possible that the basis functions you can extract from mgcv are like that, but in general this is not true; for example, the whole point of the spde/GMRF representations is that the smoothing property lies in the joint distribution of the weights, for iced, local, basis functions.
The type of smoother that is based on relatively local basis functions and independent weights is heavily dependent on the number of basis functions (leading to the problem of selecting the number of basis functions (or number of spline knots as a model selection problem).  Smoothers based on penalizing integrals of squared derivatives are less dependent on such choices, and these are the types of smoothers that are closely related to the rw1, rw2, and general Matern models.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Smooth functions like GAMs
parts:
On 13/12/2017 17:32, Finn Lindgren wrote:
Independent weights for the basis functions only gives the right model if the basis functions were constructed to allow that. It’s possible that the basis functions you can extract from mgcv are like that,

I would assume that if mgcv gives me basis functions (for a simple smoother with fixed df) that I can stick into the lm function, or obtain them via the jagam function and use them in JAGS with univariate normal priors, that I can also use them in INLA.

Finding the optimal amount of smoothing can be done the old-fashioned way (i.e. try different values)...or just stick to one value...e.g. 4 df like S-Plus did many years ago. Smoothers of covariates with cross-validation type mechanisms (like X*beta + Z*u) and spatial random fields may compete with each other anyway.

The problem I had with rw1 and rw2 smoothers is that the tend to over-fit for the data sets that I was using, which means a battle with PC priors.

Alain

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Smooth functions like GAMs
parts:
To set priors on RW1 and. RW2 use f(…, scale.model=T). As this scale it so the the precision can be interpreted as a marginal precision. There is a tutorial on this issue at r-inla.org. otherwise, there is no control of what is going on.

As Finn said, there is a reason why we haven’t implemented P-splines and friends, but use RW1/RW2 and the SPDE-models.


H
